To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adoptive transfer of dendritic cells admixed with a tumor cell inoculum is a promising approach to the treatment of cancer.

adoptive transfer of tumor cells mixed with immature DCs generates significant antitumor immunity, which is dependent upon the immunogenicity of the tumor model and is not affected by the presence or absence of tumor antigen specificity.

adoptive transfer of dendritic cells with tumor cells generates systemic immunity against a variety of mouse tumor models with undefined antigens, and that the degree of immunity generated correlates with the immunogenicity of the tumor model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of systemic antiviral and antitumor immune response by adoptive transfer in mouse models.
the generation and characterization of novel tumor vaccines.
the development of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of human cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DCs are effective in the generation of systemic antiprimordial tumor immunity, but the efficacy is dependent on the immunogenicity of the tumor model used.
the adoptive transfer strategy using DCs is effective against tumors with undefined antigens and is effective in a variety of tumor models of different immunogenicity.
the adoptive transfer approach using DCs is a promising and potentially useful immunotherapeutic modality for human cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DCs can be used to generate systemic antitumor responses, but this requires the tumor to be of moderate immunogenic potential and that the tumor be surgically excised.

the adoptive transfer protocol described here is effective only in the context of moderately immunogenic tumors and that the mechanism of action is likely to be via the priming of systemic antitumer immune responses.
DCs are capable of primed systemic antitumor responses in mouse models of varying immunogenecity, and this is not restricted to syngeneic tumors but can be extended to allogeneic tumors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunogenicity of the tumor is an important factor in the generation of systemic antiviral immune responses by adoptive transfer.
DCs are a promising vehicle for the generation of systemic anticumor immunity in a variety of tumor models.
the generation of systemic antivaccine responses is possible in mouse models of human cancer using DCs and that this is dependent on the immunogenicity of the tumor.
